title: Tutorial III.V - Modelling the Transportation Problem with JuMP
text:
Welcome to this tutorial on the transportation problem using JuMP! As always, don’t worry if you’re new to optimization - we’ll walk through everything step by step using a real-world example.
Imagine you’re running a solar panel distribution company. You have several warehouses (suppliers) and need to ship solar panels to various solar farms (customers). Each delivered truckload earns revenue, but it also causes variable costs and transportation costs. Your goal is to plan the shipments that maximize your total profit.
By the end of this tutorial, you’ll be able to:

Understand what a transportation problem is
Set up a transportation problem using JuMP
Solve the problem and interpret the results

Let’s start by loading the necessary packages:

using JuMP, HiGHS
using DataFrames, CSV

title: Tutorial III.V - Modelling the Transportation Problem with JuMP
text:
Define the variables
We can now define the variables of our model. We need to define a variable for each warehouse and solar farm pair. As before, we can use the @variable macro to define the variables. The syntax is @variable(model, varname[index1,index2] >= 0), where model is the model instance, varname is the name of the variable, and index1 and index2 are the indices of the variable. We can use vectors as input for the indices, but we could also use the keys of the dictionaries. In the following code block we mixed both options, to show you that it is possible.

# Define variable
@variable(
    transport_model,
    X[available.supplier,keys(requested_dict)] >= 0
)







Mixing indexing styles like this only works because available.supplier and keys(available_dict) contain exactly the same names - just as requested.solar_farm and keys(requested_dict) do. If one of them were a filtered DataFrame or an outdated dictionary, we would get a KeyError - or worse, a silently smaller model without any error message. In your own models, it is safer to pick one style and stick to it.

title: Tutorial III.V - Modelling the Transportation Problem with JuMP
text:
Exercise 4.1 - Define the objective
Now it is your turn to define the objective! We want to maximize the total profit: each truckload shipped from warehouse i to solar farm j earns the margin of 4700 (revenue minus variable costs) and costs the transportation costs of that route. As before, we can use the @objective macro. The syntax is @objective(model, Max, expression), where model is the model instance, Max indicates that we want to maximize the expression, and expression is the expression we want to maximize.

# YOUR CODE BELOW
# Hint: Sum over all pairs, e.g. with
# for i in keys(available_dict), j in keys(requested_dict)
# and look up the transportation costs with travelCosts_dict[(i,j)]



Code
# Test your answer
@assert objective_sense(transport_model) == MOI.MAX_SENSE "The objective should be maximized, not minimized."
@assert isapprox(
    coefficient(objective_function(transport_model), X["a_1","b_1"]),
    revenue - varCosts - travelCosts_dict[("a_1","b_1")];
    atol = 1e-6
) "The profit for each truckload from a_1 to b_1 should be the revenue minus the variable costs minus the transportation costs of that route."
println("Objective defined successfully!")

text:
Exercise 4.2 - Restrict the available truckloads
Next, we define the constraints with the @constraint macro. The first constraint ensures that each warehouse ships at most the number of truckloads it has available. Create it and name it restrictAvailable. The syntax is @constraint(model, name[index], expression), where model is the model instance, name[index] creates one constraint for each element of the index set, and expression is the expression we want to constrain. To practice the use of dictionaries, use the keys of the dictionaries for the indices here.

# YOUR CODE BELOW
# Hint: For each warehouse i, the sum of X[i,j] over all solar farms j
# has to be lower than or equal to available_dict[i]



Code
# Test your answer
@assert all(
    is_valid(transport_model, restrictAvailable[i]) for i in keys(available_dict)
) "The model should contain one constraint restrictAvailable for each warehouse."
@assert normalized_rhs(restrictAvailable["a_1"]) == available_dict["a_1"] "The right-hand side of the constraint for warehouse a_1 should be its available truckloads, $(available_dict["a_1"])."
println("Supply constraint defined successfully!")

title: Tutorial III.V - Modelling the Transportation Problem with JuMP
text:
Exercise 4.3 - Restrict the requested truckloads
The second constraint ensures that each solar farm receives at most the number of truckloads it requested. Create it and name it restrictDemand. Note the <= here: the demand is an upper limit, not an obligation. If a delivery would lose money, the model is allowed to deliver less than requested. Naturally, you could again use the keys of the dictionaries, but you could also use the vectors with the names from the DataFrames, e.g. requested.solar_farm and available.supplier, as both contain exactly the same names. You could even work with ranges from the beginning, e.g. 1:length(available.supplier) - but working with names is often more convenient.

# YOUR CODE BELOW
# Hint: For each solar farm j, the sum of X[i,j] over all warehouses i
# has to be lower than or equal to requested_dict[j]



Code
# Test your answer
@assert all(
    is_valid(transport_model, restrictDemand[j]) for j in requested.solar_farm
) "The model should contain one constraint restrictDemand for each solar farm."
@assert normalized_rhs(restrictDemand["b_1"]) == requested_dict["b_1"] "The right-hand side of the constraint for solar farm b_1 should be its requested truckloads, $(requested_dict["b_1"])."
println("Demand constraint defined successfully!")


And that’s it! We have now defined the model and can start optimizing.

title: Tutorial III.V - Modelling the Transportation Problem with JuMP
text:
Exercise 5.1 - Start optimization
Start the optimization as usual by calling the optimize! function on the model instance.

# YOUR CODE BELOW



Code
# Test your answer
@assert termination_status(transport_model) == MOI.OPTIMAL "The termination status should be OPTIMAL but is $(termination_status(transport_model))"
@assert isapprox(objective_value(transport_model), 100373406; atol = 1e-4) "The optimal profit should be 100373406 but is $(objective_value(transport_model)). Check the objective and the constraints of your model."
println("Model optimized successfully! The maximal profit is ", objective_value(transport_model), ".")


Now, we can access the values of the variables at the optimal solution. But remember, we defined the variables with the keys of the dictionaries, so we need to convert the result back to a DataFrame. If we just look at parts of the variable container, we only see the variables themselves, not their optimal values.

first(X,5)

Thus, we need to use the value function to extract the values from the variable.

transport_values = value.(X)

The result is a DenseAxisArray{Float64,2,...} with index sets. To convert it to a DataFrame, we just need to iterate over the keys of the dictionaries and store the values in a new DataFrame. As we are not interested in values which are zero, we can skip those.
First, we need to initialize an empty DataFrame with the correct column names and column types.

transport_df = DataFrame(
    supplier = String[],
    solar_farm = String[],
    truckloads = Float64[]
)

Then, we can iterate over the keys of the dictionaries and store the values in the DataFrame if they are greater than zero.

for i in keys(available_dict)
    for j in keys(requested_dict)
        if transport_values[i,j] > 0
            push!(transport_df, (
                supplier = i,
                solar_farm = j,
                truckloads = transport_values[i,j]
                )
            )
        end
    end
end

Finally, we can print the first few rows of the transportation plan to check if it looks correct.

println("Beginning of the transportation plan:")
first(transport_df,5)







Although the above code looks rather complicated, it is essentially just iterating over the keys of the dictionaries and storing the values in a new DataFrame. This is a common pattern in optimization, as we often want to convert the result of an optimization problem into a more convenient format for reporting or further processing.









We defined \(X_{i,j}\) as a continuous variable, so fractional truckloads would be allowed in the plan. If you look at the results, you will see whole truckloads everywhere anyway - a well-known property of transportation problems with whole-numbered supply and demand. In other problems, you might have to decide whether fractional values are acceptable or whether you need integer variables.

text:
Exercise 6.1 - Check the delivered truckloads
Does that mean some solar farms receive less than they requested? Find out yourself: compute the total number of truckloads delivered in the optimal plan and save it in a variable called total_delivered.

# YOUR CODE BELOW
# Hint: Use sum() on the truckloads column of transport_df



Code
# Test your answer
@assert isapprox(total_delivered, sum(requested.truckload_demand); atol = 1e-4) "total_delivered should be $(sum(requested.truckload_demand)) but is $(total_delivered). Did you sum the truckloads column of transport_df?"
println("Correct! All ", sum(requested.truckload_demand), " requested truckloads are delivered.")


Surprised? Although two thirds of all routes are unprofitable, every solar farm still receives everything it requested. Two properties of our data explain this: every solar farm has at least one route with costs below the margin (the cheapest route to any farm costs at most 1,932), and the total supply of 30,321 truckloads exceeds the total demand of 28,014. Keep in mind that this is a property of this particular data set, not a guarantee of the model. If the margin were smaller - say, the variable costs rose above 10,000 - some farms would no longer have any profitable route, and the model would leave their demand unmet.

title: Tutorial III.I - Introduction to Mathematical Optimization with JuMP and HiGHS
text:
Welcome to this beginner-friendly tutorial on mathematical optimization using JuMP and the HiGHS solver in Julia! Don’t worry if these terms sound unfamiliar – we’ll explain everything step by step.
In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to:

Set up a simple optimization problem
Define variables and constraints
Create an objective function
Solve the problem and interpret the results

We’ll use a real-world example to make these concepts more relatable. Imagine you’re managing a small factory that produces two types of products. Your goal is to maximize profit while working within certain limitations. This is exactly the kind of problem that mathematical optimization can solve!


JuMP (Julia for Mathematical Programming) is a powerful tool that helps us describe optimization problems in a way that computers can understand and solve. Think of it as a translator between your business problem and the mathematical solver.



HiGHS is an open-source solver that can find solutions to the optimization problems we describe using JuMP. It’s like a very smart calculator that can handle complex problems quickly and efficiently.



Let’s break down our factory management problem:

You produce two products: Product A and Product B
Each product gives you a different profit:

Product A: 100 profit per unit
Product B: 150 profit per unit

You have two departments: Cutting and Finishing
Each product requires different amounts of time in each department:

Product A: 2 hours in Cutting, 4 hours in Finishing
Product B: 4 hours in Cutting, 3 hours in Finishing

You have limited time available in each department:

Cutting: 40 hours total
Finishing: 60 hours total


Your goal is to decide how many of each product to make to maximize your total profit, while not exceeding the available time in each department.



First, we need to install and load the necessary packages. If you haven’t already installed JuMP and HiGHS, you can do so by running import Pkg and then Pkg.add(["JuMP","HiGHS"]).
Now, let’s load these packages:

using JuMP, HiGHS

Great! We’re now ready to start building our optimization model.

Julia uses short-circuit evaluation for && and || operators. This means that the second operand is only evaluated if necessary.



Let’s see short-circuiting in action:

x = 0
(x != 0) && (1/x > 1)

false


Because x != 0 is already false, the whole && expression must be false - so Julia never computes 1/x and no division by zero happens. You will often see this pattern in real Julia code, for example condition && error("Something went wrong").

pattern = "(lowering|inference)/undef-global-var"

severity = "off"
path = "**/tutorial-*.jl"

section: Packages do not install or load. What can I do?
text:
Packages do not install or load. What can I do?

could not download https://pkg.julialang.org/registries, failed to clone from https://github.com/JuliaRegistries/General.git or Unable to automatically download/install artifact. Julia cannot reach its package servers. Check that the internet works in your browser and try again, or switch to another network such as a phone hotspot. If it still fails, run ENV["JULIA_PKG_SERVER"] = "" in Julia before Pkg.add(...): Pkg then downloads from GitHub instead.
The following 1 package failed to precompile or Failed to precompile Plots. A package cache is broken, often after an interrupted first using. Close Zed and any other Julia window, delete the folder .julia/compiled/v1.13 in your user folder (Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.julia\compiled\v1.13), start Julia in your workshop folder with julia --project=. and run using Pkg; Pkg.precompile().
Package JuMP [...] is required but does not seem to be installed. The workshop environment lists the package, but its files are missing, for example after you copied your workshop folder to another laptop. Start Julia in your workshop folder with julia --project=. and run using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate().
The active manifest file has dependencies that were resolved with a different julia version. You set up the workshop environment with another Julia version. Close Zed and check that julia --version shows 1.13. Then run steps 3 and 5 of the first tutorial again, with using Pkg; Pkg.resolve() in between.
Unsatisfiable requirements detected for package. The package versions do not fit together, often because the package list on your laptop is out of date. Run using Pkg; Pkg.update() in the workshop environment. If the error names a package the workshop does not use, remove it with Pkg.rm("Name").
No space left on device. The .julia folder in your user folder grows by several GB over time. Run using Pkg; Pkg.gc() and delete the compiled folders of Julia versions you no longer use, such as .julia/compiled/v1.10.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Julia or Zed does not work on my Windows laptop. What can I do?
text:
Julia or Zed does not work on my Windows laptop. What can I do?

The terminal does not find julia. Open a new terminal; if you use the terminal inside Zed, restart Zed. If that does not help, open Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases and switch on julia.exe and juliaup.exe. If the Microsoft Store is blocked on your laptop, use the MSI installer instead.
“Program ‘julia.exe’ failed to run: The file cannot be accessed by the system”. An installation through the Microsoft Store, winget or the MSIX App Installer did not finish and left a broken alias for julia.exe behind. The same alias makes ;julia inside Julia fail with permission denied (EACCES). Uninstall Julia under Settings → Apps → Installed apps. If you also installed a standalone version such as the 1.10 LTS, uninstall it too: the workshop runs Julia 1.13 through juliaup. If julia still shows the error, switch off julia.exe and juliaup.exe under Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases. Then install Julia with the MSI installer and open a new terminal; if you use the terminal inside Zed, restart Zed. If you had already installed the workshop kernel, run steps 3 and 5 of the first tutorial again.
Access is denied. (os error 5) or Failed to move extracted archive while Julia installs itself. Your antivirus scans the freshly unpacked files and blocks juliaup. Run the same command again (julia or juliaup add release): it usually works on the second or third try. Delete leftover julia-temp-... folders in %USERPROFILE%\.julia\juliaup. If you use an antivirus other than Microsoft Defender, add %USERPROFILE%\.julia as an exception.
julia --version shows an old version such as 1.10, or Zed offers the kernel optimization-with-julia-1.10. Another Julia comes first, usually a standalone installation. Run where.exe julia in PowerShell to see all of them. Uninstall every “Julia 1.x.y” entry under Settings → Apps → Installed apps and keep the one called “Julia” (juliaup). Then run juliaup add release and juliaup default release, open a new terminal or restart Zed, and run steps 3 and 5 of the first tutorial again.
Installing from the Microsoft Store or with winget fails with an error code. 0x80073D01 or “blocked by policy”: your laptop does not allow the Store, so use the MSI installer. 0x80073CF4: drive C: is full; free some space. 0x80073CF3 or 0x80073CFB: an older Julia is in the way; uninstall Julia under Settings → Apps → Installed apps and try again.
The Julia launcher failed to figure out which juliaup channel to use or Io error. Look inside err_kind for more details. Julia is installed, but no Julia version inside it, often because the laptop was offline at the first start. Check your internet connection and run juliaup add release and juliaup default release. If that fails, uninstall Julia, delete the folder %USERPROFILE%\.julia\juliaup, restart Windows and install Julia again.
“An Application Control policy has blocked this file”, “Smart App Control has blocked part of this app” or error 0xc0e90002. Windows Smart App Control blocks the package files that Julia compiles on your laptop. Switch it off under Windows Security → App & browser control → Smart App Control and keep it off while you work with Julia: switched on again, it can block every package Julia compiles later. Then delete the folder %USERPROFILE%\.julia\compiled\v1.13 and run using Pkg; Pkg.precompile() in the workshop environment. On a laptop managed by your university or employer, only the IT department can allow these files; until then, start Julia in your workshop folder with julia --pkgimages=no --project=. in the first tutorial and add "--pkgimages=no" right after the --project argument of its installkernel call. Packages then load more slowly, but they load.
Precompiling IJulia fails with an EPIPE error. Run using IJulia again: the error is known on Windows and usually disappears on the second attempt.
Your laptop has a Snapdragon (ARM) processor. Julia runs there in x64 emulation: the workshop setup should work the same way, only slower.
Your workshop folder lies in OneDrive. Synced folders can block Julia from replacing files. Use a plain folder such as C:\Users\<name>\julia-workshop.

text:
Julia does not work on my Mac or Linux laptop. What can I do?

zsh: command not found: julia or bash: julia: command not found right after the install. The terminal was open before the install and has not read the new settings. Close all terminal windows and Zed, then open a new terminal. If that does not help, run . ~/.zshrc (macOS) or . ~/.bashrc (Linux). If juliaup works but julia does not, run juliaup self update; if that does not help, run the install command again.
julia --version shows another version than 1.13. An older Julia from Homebrew or a .dmg download comes first. Run which -a julia to see all of them. Keep juliaup’s: ~/.juliaup/bin/julia, or /opt/homebrew/bin/julia if you installed juliaup with brew install juliaup. Remove the others, for example with brew uninstall julia, by moving Julia-1.x.app from Applications to the Trash, or with sudo rm /usr/local/bin/julia if that path is listed. Then open a new terminal and run steps 3 and 5 of the first tutorial again.
Ubuntu suggests sudo snap install julia or sudo apt install julia. Don’t: these packages are outdated. Use the install command from julialang.org/downloads. If it stops with curl: (23) Failure writing output to destination, your curl comes from snap: run sudo snap remove curl and sudo apt install curl, then run the install command again.
Permission denied (os error 13) while installing or starting Julia. Files in your user folder belong to the administrator, usually because Julia once ran with sudo. Run sudo chown -R "$(whoami)" ~/.julia ~/.juliaup, then start Julia without sudo. Never use sudo for julia or Pkg.

Still stuck? Ask the course chatbot on this website: it knows these steps.

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text: This cheatsheet provides a quick reference for Julia programming language syntax and common operations. Julia is a high-level, high-performance programming language designed for numerical and scientific computing. It combines the ease of use of Python or R with the speed of C. For comprehensive documentation, visit:

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Variable Declaration and Types

# Basic variable declaration
x = 1                  # Implicit typing
y::Int64 = 5          # Explicit type annotation

# Common types
num_int = 42          # Integer (Int64)
num_float = 19.99     # Float (Float64)
is_student = true     # Boolean
name = "Julia"        # String
c = 3 + 4im           # Complex number
sym = :symbol         # Symbol

# Check type
typeof(num_int)       # Returns Int64
typeof(num_float)     # Returns Float64

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
String Operations

# String manipulation
str = "Hello, World!"
length(str)           # String length
lowercase(str)        # Convert to lowercase
uppercase(str)        # Convert to uppercase
strip(" text ")       # Remove leading/trailing whitespace

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
String Interpolation

name = "Julia"
age = 30
# Basic interpolation
msg1 = "I am $age years old"
# Expression interpolation
msg2 = "In 5 years, I'll be $(age + 5)"
# Complex interpolation
greeting = "Hello, my name is $name and I am $age years old"

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Type Conversion

# Convert between types
float_num = Float64(42)    # Int to Float
int_num = Int64(3.14)      # Float to Int
str_num = string(42)       # Number to String

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Vectors

# Create vectors
grades = [95, 87, 91, 78, 88]    # Numeric vector
names = ["Mike", "Yola", "Elio"] # String vector

# Vector operations
push!(grades, 82)       # Add element to end
pop!(grades)           # Remove last element
popfirst!(grades)      # Remove first element

# Vector indexing
first = grades[1]      # Access first element
subset = grades[1:3]   # Access first three elements

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Matrices

# Create matrices
matrix = [1 2 3; 4 5 6]    # 2x3 matrix
# Matrix operations
matrix[2,3] = 17           # Change specific element

# Matrix arithmetic
matrix1 = [2 2; 3 3]
matrix2 = [1 2; 3 4]
sum_matrix = matrix1 + matrix2      # Matrix addition
prod_matrix = matrix1 * matrix2     # Matrix multiplication
element_prod = matrix1 .* matrix2   # Element-wise multiplication

# Broadcasting
matrix .+ 10                # Add 10 to each element

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Tuples

# Create tuples (immutable)
person = ("Elio Smith", 18, "Hamburg")
rgb = (255, 0, 0)

# Tuple operations
name = person[1]           # Access first element
age, city = person[2:3]    # Multiple assignment

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Key Differences

Vectors: Mutable, 1-dimensional, good for lists
Matrices: Mutable, 2-dimensional, good for linear algebra
Tuples: Immutable, fixed-size, good for grouping related constants

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Basic Comparisons

# Comparison operators
x == y    # Equal to
x != y    # Not equal to
x < y     # Less than
x > y     # Greater than
x <= y    # Less than or equal to
x >= y    # Greater than or equal to

# Examples
password_correct = (input == "secret123")
is_adult = (age >= 18)
can_afford = (price <= budget)

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Logical Operators

# AND operator (&&)
can_buy = (age >= 18) && (money >= price)    # Both conditions must be true

# OR operator (||)
need_coat = (temp < 10) || is_raining        # At least one must be true

# NOT operator (!)
is_closed = !is_open                         # Inverts boolean value

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Chained Comparisons

# Instead of
x >= 0 && x <= 10    # Check if x is between 0 and 10

# You can write
0 <= x <= 10         # More natural syntax

# Real-world examples
normal_temp = 36.5 <= body_temp <= 37.5
work_hours = 9 <= current_hour < 17

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Key Points

Comparisons return boolean values (true or false)
&& requires all conditions to be true
|| requires at least one condition to be true
! inverts a boolean value
Chained comparisons make range checks more readable

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
For Loops

# Basic for loop with range
for i in 1:3
    println(i)        # Prints 1, 2, 3
end

# Iterating over array
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits
    println(fruit)    # Prints each fruit
end

# For loop with break
for x in 1:10
    if x == 4
        break        # Exits loop when x is 4
    end
end

# For loop with conditions
for x in 1:10
    if x <= 2
        println(x)
    elseif x == 3
        println("Three!")
    else 
        break
    end
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
While Loops

# Basic while loop
number = 10
while number >= 5
    number -= 1      # Decrements until < 5
end

# Infinite loop with break
current = 0
while true
    current += 1
    if current == 5
        break        # Exits when condition met
    end
end

# While loop with condition
lives = 3
while lives > 0
    lives -= 1       # Continues until lives = 0
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Nested Loops

# Nested loop example
sizes = ["S", "M", "L"]
colors = ["Red", "Blue"]
for size in sizes
    for color in colors
        println("$color $size")
    end
end

# Matrix iteration
for i in 1:3
    for j in 1:2
        println("Position: $i,$j")
    end
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
List Comprehensions

# Basic list comprehension
squares = [n^2 for n in 1:5]    # [1,4,9,16,25]

# With condition
evens = [n for n in 1:10 if n % 2 == 0]    # [2,4,6,8,10]

# Nested comprehension
matrix = [i*j for i in 1:3, j in 1:3]    # 3x3 multiplication table

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Key Points

for loops are best when you know the number of iterations
while loops are useful for unknown iteration counts
Use break to exit loops early
List comprehensions offer concise array creation
Nested loops are useful for multi-dimensional iteration

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Basic Dictionary Operations

# Create a dictionary
student_ids = Dict(
    "Elio" => 1001,
    "Bob" => 1002,
    "Yola" => 1003
)

# Access values
id = student_ids["Elio"]        # Get value by key
student_ids["David"] = 1004     # Add new key-value pair
delete!(student_ids, "Bob")     # Remove entry

# Check key existence
if haskey(student_ids, "Eve")
    println(student_ids["Eve"])
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Advanced Operations

# Dictionary with array values
grades = Dict(
    "Elio" => [85, 92, 78],
    "Bob" => [76, 88, 94]
)

# Get all keys and values
names = keys(grades)          # Get all keys
scores = values(grades)       # Get all values

# Iterate over dictionary
for (student, grade_list) in grades
    avg = sum(grade_list) / length(grade_list)
    println("$student: $avg")
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Common Methods

# Dictionary methods
length(dict)           # Number of entries
empty!(dict)           # Remove all entries
get(dict, key, default)# Get value or default if key missing
merge(dict1, dict2)    # Combine two dictionaries
copy(dict)             # Create shallow copy

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Key Points

Keys must be unique
Values can be of any type (including arrays)
Use haskey() to safely check for key existence
Dictionaries are mutable (can be changed)
Keys are accessed with square brackets dict["key"]

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Basic Function Definition

# Basic function with explicit return
function say_hello(name)
    return "Hello, $(name)!"
end

# Function with implicit return
function multiply(a, b)
    a * b    # Last expression is automatically returned
end

# Conditional return
function do_something(a, b)
    if a > b
        return a * b
    else
        return a + b
    end
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Advanced Function Features

# Optional arguments
function greet(name="Guest", greeting="Hello")
    "$greeting, $name!"
end

# Multiple return values
function stats(numbers)
    avg = sum(numbers) / length(numbers)
    min_val = minimum(numbers)
    max_val = maximum(numbers)
    return avg, min_val, max_val
end

# Anonymous functions
numbers = 1:10
map(x -> x^2, numbers)  # Square each number

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Function Scope

# Local scope example
function bake_cake()
    secret_ingredient = "vanilla"    # Only exists inside function
    return secret_ingredient        # Must return to access outside
end

# Variables outside function not accessible inside
global_var = 10
function scope_example()
    # Can read global_var but can't modify it
    return global_var + 5
end

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Multiple Dispatch

# Generic operation for all types
function operation(a, b)
    "Generic operation for $(typeof(a)) and $(typeof(b))"
end

# Type-specific implementations
operation(a::Number, b::Number) = a + b        # For numbers
operation(a::String, b::String) = string(a, b) # For strings

# Usage examples
operation(10, 20)          # Returns 30
operation("Hello", "!")    # Returns "Hello!"
operation("Hi", 42)        # Uses generic operation

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Key Points

Functions can have explicit or implicit returns
Last expression is automatically returned if no return statement
Variables inside functions are local by default
Multiple dispatch allows different behavior based on argument types
Use return for early exits or conditional

title: Julia Syntax Cheatsheet
text:
Basic Package Operations

# Import package manager
import Pkg              # Access as Pkg.function()
using Pkg              # Import all exported names

# Add packages
Pkg.add("DataFrames")  # Add single package
Pkg.add(["Package1", "Package2"])  # Add multiple packages

# Update packages
Pkg.update()           # Update all packages
Pkg.update("DataFrames")  # Update specific package

# Remove packages
Pkg.rm("DataFrames")   # Remove package

title: Welcome to Optimization with Julia!
text:
Description
This small workshop will introduce you to the basics of mathematical optimization using Julia. Throughout the workshop, you will learn the basics of Julia and JuMP, the de facto standard for mathematical optimization in Julia. We will work with simple, practical examples to help you understand the core concepts. You will learn how to formulate basic optimization problems and translate them into code. The workshop was originally part of the course Applied Optimization but it is now also offered as a standalone small workshop.


Learning Outcomes
My goal is to introduce you to the Julia programming language and the JuMP package for mathematical optimization. Both are widely used in academia and industry and are great tools to know. Julia is a fast, flexible, and powerful programming language that is becoming more and more popular in academia and industry. JuMP is a package that allows you to formulate and solve optimization problems in Julia, it is an alternative to other popular optimization software such as GAMS, AMPL, Pyomo, etc.
Upon completion of the workshop, you will be able to:

Apply the basics of the Julia programming language
Implement basic optimization problems in Julia
Understand the core concepts of optimization
Apply optimization techniques to practical problems

Please note that this workshop is designed to be accessible to everyone, including complete beginners. No advanced knowledge or experience in programming is required to follow along, although knowledge of programming is helpful! The teaching format accommodates different levels of programming skills, ensuring that every participant can get the most out of the workshop.


Course Blocks
The core content of the workshop is organized in four blocks:

Introduction
Part I: Variables and Types
Part II: Functions, Data Frames and Plots
Part III: Optimization with JuMP



Tutorials
The workshop is organized in a series of tutorials. Each tutorial is a self-contained document that you can download and run locally.

You can find the content for each part in the corresponding folder
To run the code, download the tutorial as a .jl file (the Julia link on each page) and work through it cell by cell in Zed; the introduction walks you through installing Julia and Zed, and the first tutorial through the workshop’s package environment and the Jupyter kernel
Each tutorial is also available as a Jupyter notebook (the Jupyter link on each page), if you prefer to work with .ipynb files
If you cannot install anything on your machine, you can still read every tutorial here on the website: all results are already executed on the pages



AI Policy
Course chatbot. A course chatbot is available on this website for exploratory study. It is designed to guide your problem-solving process rather than hand out answers: expect hints and questions back, not finished solutions. It runs on EU-hosted infrastructure (Mistral models, servers in Germany), and your conversations are not used to train models. Details are on the privacy page.
External AI tools. You may use external AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Mistral, Gemini). You are responsible for every line of code you rely on: understand what the AI produced before you build on it. Letting AI solve the exercises for you defeats their purpose.
No graded submissions. This workshop has no graded hand-ins and no exam; the exercises and self-checks are for you. The only person an AI shortcut cheats here is yourself.


Questions

text:
Welcome to this tutorial on advanced solver options in JuMP using the HiGHS solver! Don’t worry if “advanced solver options” sounds intimidating - we’ll break everything down into simple, easy-to-understand concepts.
Imagine you’re using a GPS app to find the best route to a new restaurant. Just like how you can adjust settings in your GPS (like avoiding toll roads or preferring highways), we can adjust settings in our optimization solver to help it find solutions more efficiently or to meet specific requirements.
By the end of this tutorial, you’ll be able to:

Understand what solver options are and why they’re useful
Set basic solver options like time limits and solution tolerances
Interpret solver output to understand how well your problem was solved

section: Exercise 2.1 - Modify and Solve the Problem
text:
Exercise 2.1 - Modify and Solve the Problem
Now it’s your turn! Modify the problem above by:

Changing the production time constraint to 300 minutes
Increasing the profit for widgets to 30
Solving the modified problem and printing the results







Re-initializing with Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) gives you a completely fresh model. Remember from Section 1 that solver options belong to the model - the time limit, MIP gap, and presolve settings you set earlier are gone, and you would have to set them again if you need them.




# YOUR CODE BELOW
# Hint: Copy the code above and make the necessary changes
model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) # Don't forget to re-initialize the model



Code
# Test your answer
@assert termination_status(model) == MOI.OPTIMAL "The termination status should be OPTIMAL but is $(termination_status(model))"
@assert isapprox(objective_value(model), 3780, atol=1e-6) "The objective value should be 3780 but is $(objective_value(model))"
println("Excellent work! You've successfully modified and solved the optimization problem.")








Why does the test only check the profit and not the number of widgets and gadgets? Because the modified problem has several optimal plans: 80 widgets and 46 gadgets, 79 and 47, and 78 and 48 all respect the time limit and earn exactly 3780. Both products now bring in the same profit per unit, so the solver is free to return any of these plans - which one you get depends on the solver’s internal path. Whenever a problem can have several optimal solutions, test the objective value, not the variable values.
